newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 16.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The Australian Tax Office will attempt to toughen up the tax system following the discovery that collections from small companies were running A$639 million short of Budget estimates at the end of January, leaving the Federal Government with a damaging shortfall. The ATO is concerned the current tax system has developed serious compliance problems. Page 1.

The so-called "millennium bug" is expected to cost large Australian companies A$200 million or more each, yet is seen as a huge boost for ageing computer programmers, who can expect their salaries to double over the next few years. Existing software not configured for the new century will need to be rewritten in a language called Cobol, but few software programmers know how to work with it. Page 1.

Aboriginal leaders have provided Prime Minister John Howard with legal advice stating that both Howard's plan and the National Party proposal to extinguish native title rights could be contested in the High Court as either plan breached the Racial Discrimnation Act. Page 3.

Coal & Allied, a subsidiary of RTZ-CRA, yesterday applied for a certificate from the Australian Industrial Relations Commission to allow it to take Federal Court action against unions and individual union officers for damages over industrial action at its Hunter Valley No. 1 mine. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Government Senate Leader Robert Hill said yesterday he will block a Senate inquiry into rorts allegations against Independent Senator Mal Colston given that the allegations have been referred to the Australian Federal Police. Hill said he thinks the police should be able to get on with the job and believes the Privileges Committee, which would investigate the affair, would not add much to the process. Page 1.

Ken Cowley, who has led News Limited for 18 years and is one of Australia's longest-serving and most successful business leaders, will step down from his position in June. In what he calls his "gutsiest decision", Cowley's resignation has been met with regret by Rupert Murdoch, Kerry Packer and Prime Minister John Howard. Page 1.

The United States has called on the Howard Government to reverse its decision to withhold support for a United Nations Human Rights Commission censure of China. For the first time in six years, Australia will not support the motion, but will hold closed-door talks with China on the issue. Page 1.

Following a briefing with Federal Cabinet yesterday, Prime Minister John Howard told the Queensland Liberal Party farmers will not be let down in the Federal Government's response to the High Court's Wik decision. Howard told Cabinet yesterday he believe the response would be welcomed by Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge, who has taken a hard-line stance on the issue. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer has refused to give in to pressure from United States Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to support a United Nations resolution condemning China's human rights record. In an amicable discussion, Downer told Albright he felt previous resolutions were not successful and other avenues needed to be taken with China. Page 1.

The tradition of the Anzacs sold out for A$20,000 yesterday under an agreement with Super League and the Returned Services League. The agreement will see a rugby league match staged between Australia and New Zealand on Anzac Day, giving the RSL access to the youth market, and the A$20,000 contribution to its construction of the Kokoda memorial walkway at Rhodes Park, Concord. Page 1.

Following estimates by researchers at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne that of 1,200 hysterectomies and sterilisations of young women with intellectual disabilities since 1992, only 20 had Family Court approval, the Family Court has warned doctos performing such procedures may face prosecutions if they are done outside the law. Page 1.

The Wallis report into Australia's financial system yesterday faced criticism from the National Farmers' Federation, which claimed the inquiry turned its back on rural people, many of whom had to drive hundreds of kilometres to do their banking, and the Astralian Consumers Association, which described the report as being full of promises with no detail. Page 1.
THE AGE

An Age investigation has found nothing was done by Victorian authorities to assist thousands of the State's children who were unnecessarily made wards of the State and sent to non-Government institutions over two decades, even though it was known some of the children were routinely beaten, starved, humiliated, and emotionally abused. Page 1.

Several former wards of the State have outlined the kind of torture they went through while staying at St Catherine's Children's Home in Geelong in the 1950s and 1960s, including being shoved underwater by nuns to be calmed down. Many of the women still carry emotional, and for at least one, physical, scars from their time at the home. Page 1.

In a submission delivered to Prime Minister John Howard on Monday night, Aboriginal leaders said they will make some concessions on the Federal Government's response to the Wik decision, but they will challenge Howard's threat to extinguish native title by refusing to accept his plan for dealing with the issue. Page 1.

Under plan to fight drink-driving being considered in Victoria, repeat offenders will be forced to fit an interlock device to their cars that would not allow the vehicle to start if alcohol was detected on the driver's breath. The device, known as Breathlyzer, was developed by Melbourne company Drager Australia in conjunction with Vic Roads and has been successfully tested by the RACV. Page 1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
